title: Κολοιὸς καὶ ἀλώπηξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 160. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κολοιὸς λιμώττων ἐπί τινος συκῆς ἐκάθισεν· εὑρὼν δὲ τοὺς ὀλύνθους μηδέπω πεπείρους προσέμενεν ἕως σῦκα γένωνται.
sentences.tr: Koloios limōttōn epi tinos sykēs ekathisen· heurōn de tous olynthous mēdepō pepeirous prosemenen heōs syka genōntai.
sentences.l: A jackdaw, starving, settled upon a fig tree; and having found the green figs not yet ripe, he waited until they should become figs.
sentences.n: ὄλυνθος is the fig that sets out of season and hangs on the tree without ever ripening into a σῦκον, a true fig — so waiting for the ὄλυνθοι to 'become figs' is a wait that cannot end, and the fable's whole point sits in that one word. ἕως with the subjunctive and no ἄν looks forward to an event expected but not yet in hand.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ θεασαμένη αὐτὸν ἐγχρονίζοντα καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν παρ’ αὐτοῦ μαθοῦσα ἔφη· « Ἀλλὰ πεπλάνησαι, ὦ οὗτος, ἐλπίδι προσέχων, ἥτις βουκολεῖν μὲν οἶδε, τρέφειν δὲ οὐδαμῶς. »
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de theasamenē auton enchronizonta kai tēn aitian par’ autou mathousa ephē· « Alla peplanēsai, ō houtos, elpidi prosechōn, hētis boukolein men oide, trephein de oudamōs. »
sentences.l: But a fox, having watched him lingering and having learned the reason from him, said: « But you are led astray, you there, in holding to hope, which knows how to beguile, but to feed by no means. »
sentences.i: But a fox watched him lingering, and when she had learned the reason from him, said: « You are deluded, you there, in clinging to hope — she knows how to lead a creature on, but to feed it, not at all. »
sentences.n: βουκολέω is 'to herd cattle', and so, in the metaphor, to drive a man about at will and put him off with expectations. πεπλάνησαι is a perfect passive of πλανάω, 'you have been set wandering', the state you are now in. προσέχων has νοῦν understood: 'holding your mind to'. θεασαμένη … ἐγχρονίζοντα is a verb of perceiving with the supplementary participle, seeing him in the act.

Square brackets are Chambry's mark for words he judges to have crept in later and would delete — the opposite of the angle brackets he keeps for his own additions. Here the whole moral stands inside them; compare fable 33, where a whole opening sentence is bracketed the same way. The line is printed as it stands on his page, brackets and all. φιλόνεικος is 'fond of victory, contentious', which sits oddly on a fable about a bird undone by hope; why Chambry judged the line an addition he does not say. The moral is of the bare kind — πρός with the accusative naming a target, and no verb written at all.
